title: INTC Stock Dips Even After CEO Lip-Bu Tan Buys $9.7M Worth Of Intel Shares
detail:
INTC Stock Dips Even After CEO Lip-Bu Tan Buys $9.7M Worth Of Intel Shares
Shashank Nayar
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 2:07 PM MST 3 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Chief Executive Officer Lip-Bu Tan purchased 150,000 shares of common stock across multiple trades priced between $64.71 and $64.74.

The strategic share acquisition follows Intel's Q3 2026 earnings release, which showed $16.5 billion in revenue, but shares suffered a sharp after-hours plunge driven by conservative fourth-quarter sales forecasts.

Investors are weighing cooling artificial intelligence capital expenditure (capex) cycles following a Democratic wave in mid-term elections.

Intel's (INTC) chief executive officer and director Lip-Bu Tan acquired 150,000 shares of common stock worth $9.7 million on Nov. 2 via his family trust, according to a regulatory filing on Wednesday.

Tan bought the stock through several open-market transactions at prices ranging from $64.705 to $64.735; the total investment amounted to approximately $9.71 million. The move could be seen as a vote of confidence as the semiconductor giant navigates supply chain pressures, fabrication hurdles at its Israel facility, and shifting demand in the personal computer market.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Following this acquisition, Tan's indirect holdings have climbed to roughly 1.46 million shares.

INTC stock fell about 4% on Wednesday.

Q3 Financials And Conservative Outlook

The insider purchase arrives on the heels of Intel's third-quarter fiscal 2026 financial report, where the chipmaker beat Q3 earnings expectations, but the stock faced intense selling pressure after the company furnished softer-than-expected Q4 guidance.

Q4 sales were projected to land between $15 billion and $16 billion, falling well short of analyst expectations. The company continues to face headwinds in foundry profitability, gross margin compression, and the hyper-competitive data center landscape as rivals scale up artificial intelligence capabilities.

The client computing division, its largest revenue contributor, brought in $8.1 billion during the third quarter, a 5% year-over-year revenue drop.

However, fourth-quarter projections point to steeper declines. Executive leadership anticipates client sales will plummet over 20% quarter-over-quarter, with Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner noting that PC market sluggishness could drag on through the first half of 2027.

Furthermore, Wall Street investors are increasingly betting that a Democratic-led legislative agenda could introduce tighter oversight, potentially helping to rein in aggressive artificial intelligence capital expenditure (capex).

Goldman Sachs' $675 Target Says AMD's Selloff Went Too Far ©Alexander's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Goldman Sachs trimmed its AMD price target to $675 from $700 and kept its Buy rating, a target 40% above Tuesday's close.

AMD shares are 28% below their October high after worries over AI spending and Intel's weak PC guidance, even as AMD now expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027.

Goldman's target works out to 60x the earnings analysts expect over the next twelve months, near AMD's June peak and well above its 5-year average of 35x.

The target looks reachable in a year if AMD earns what analysts expect for 2027, though that depends on a few AI labs getting their data centers running on time.

Goldman Sachs trimmed its price target on Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) to $675 from $700 on Wednesday and kept its Buy rating, after AMD's record third quarter. That's 40% above Tuesday's close of $483.90, with the stock 28% below its Oct. 6 closing high.

A rough October for AI chips

AMD's slide began in mid-October, when a selloff in CoreWeave's bonds and questions about OpenAI's revenue revived worries about who pays for the AI build-out.

Then Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, with client revenue down more than 20% from the third quarter. AMD lost 11% on Oct. 30 on Intel's PC warning.

Goldman still likes it best

AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion, and Data Center revenue nearly doubled to $8.5 billion. AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion, above the roughly $16.2 billion that analysts' full-year forecasts implied going in.

On the call, CEO Lisa Su went further: "we now expect revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027."

Goldman's James Schneider expects the stock "to trade higher following stronger results and guidance which we believe supports our bullish revenue growth outlook for AMD through 2027," and called AMD "our favorite idea in the group." Goldman cut its target because of valuation.

Strategy (MSTR:NASDAQ) stock is up 7% today, riding a Bitcoin rally and a broad market lift after Tuesday's midterm elections.

BitMine Immersion Technologies (BMNR:NYSE), which owns 4.9% of all ether, rode the same wave.

CEO Phong Le wrote on X that Strategy ranks fourth among US companies selling stock in 2026, behind only SpaceX, Alphabet and Intel, after finishing first in 2025.

"The AI investment cycle is massive. So is the Bitcoin capital cycle," Le wrote.

Strategy moves faster than Bitcoin

Bitcoin was up about 3.5% by midday, so today's jump is roughly twice as big. That fits the balance sheet: Strategy's bitcoin was worth 1.6x its common book value at June 30.

The cushion is thin, though. Monday's filing shows 849,327 bitcoin at an average cost of $75,451 a coin, and even today's rally only takes Bitcoin to around $80,500.

Strategy books bitcoin's price swings as profit or loss, so analysts' earnings estimates lurch between big gains and big losses:

Those sales add bitcoin per share only when the stock trades well above its bitcoin's value. Le put that multiple at 1.15x on the third-quarter call, under management's 1.22x break-even. And preferred dividends of about $1.76 billion a year never stop.

BitMine runs the same playbook with ether. It jumped 8% today, and it said Monday it held 6,060,506 ether, after adding 8,573 last week. Its shares are also down 58% over the past year: the same leverage in reverse.

Greg Abbott in Texas, where MARA's 2-gigawatt Matagorda County site still awaits ERCOT and interconnect approvals. Does a new governor slow those down? MARA reports on Nov. 9.

title: AMD Stock Rebounds. Is Its AI Edge Built to Last?
detail:
AMD Stock Rebounds. Is Its AI Edge Built to Last?
The Rule Breakers Team, The Motley Fool

By Nov. 2, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) had dropped about 28% from its Oct. 6 record close. Then, after the market closed yesterday, the chipmaker reported that its data center sales had nearly doubled from a year ago. It also forecast fourth-quarter revenue about two-thirds higher than the same quarter last year. The stock rose about 5% in pre-market trading this morning.

Team Rule Breakers recommended AMD in Stock Advisor on Jan. 18, 2024, at $162.67, weeks after the company launched its MI300 AI chips. At the time, AMD's edge over Intel in server processors was well established, and arguably its AI business had barely begun. The stock has roughly tripled since, and it's comfortably ahead of the S&P 500. Team Rule Breakers and Team Hidden Gems have recommended AMD across eight active Motley Fool services, and it has never carried a sell recommendation.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The second of six Rule Breakers Traits is: Sustainable Competitive Advantage.

This trait asks how a company will keep beating its rivals over the next decade. The advantage can come from a network that gets more valuable as it grows, from patents, from strong leaders, or from rivals that fail to keep up. A company can also have a lasting edge in one business and little or none in another, as AMD's latest report indicates.

Where AMD Outbuilt Intel

For years, AMD and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have fought over the processors that run data center servers. AMD builds each processor from several small chips, called chiplets, and joins them in one package. Small chips tend to have fewer defects than one large chip, so more of them come out usable. That can help AMD sell more computing power per dollar.

Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has steadily won share from Intel by many measures, and Intel's stock fell nearly 29% on Oct. 30 after a weak forecast.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

A Costlier Fight in AI Chips

AMD's position in AI chips is newer and likely less secure. It sells them to OpenAI, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). Management expects AI sales to pass server processor sales for the first time this quarter. But AMD effectively paid to land two of its biggest deals.

It gave OpenAI and Meta warrants for up to 160 million shares each, or about 20% of its share count combined. The warrants are generally tied to how many AMD chips those customers deploy and to AMD's stock price.

title: Is Broadcom Stock a Buy Now?

Is Broadcom Stock a Buy Now?
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool

AVGO
NVDA
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) has had a rough year on Wall Street, with shares falling 31% from their all-time high and down 4% since the beginning of 2026. The latest setback came Friday, when Intel's disappointing fourth-quarter guidance triggered a broad sell-off in semiconductor stocks.

But there's an interesting disconnect between Broadcom's stock performance and its actual business results. And I think investors should be paying attention.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Back in August, I argued that Broadcom could be a compelling buy if its fiscal third-quarter earnings showed $16 billion in artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor revenue, followed by guidance for continued growth.

Well, the results are in. And Broadcom delivered.

Image source: Getty Images.
Broadcom's AI business is firing on all cylinders

Broadcom reported $16.7 billion in AI semiconductor revenue for its fiscal third quarter, beating management's $16 billion target. That represented a whopping 221% increase from a year ago and 54% growth from the previous quarter.

And the outlook was even better.

CEO Hock Tan projected AI semiconductor revenue of $21.7 billion in the fourth quarter, representing 236% year-over-year growth. Overall, Broadcom reported third-quarter revenue of $29.6 billion, up 86%, and generated $13.7 billion in free cash flow. Those are outstanding numbers, particularly for a company whose stock has struggled this year.

One of my concerns in August was whether Broadcom's relationship with Alphabet could be threatened by Google's expanding partnership with Marvell Technology. Broadcom helps design Google's custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), which offer an alternative to Nvidia's more versatile graphics processing units.

The Marvell agreement raised questions about whether Broadcom could lose business. But the third-quarter results and fourth-quarter guidance suggest demand for Broadcom's custom AI accelerators and networking products remains exceptionally strong.

That doesn't eliminate the competitive risk. It does, however, make it much harder to defend the argument that Broadcom's growth is already faltering.

Is Broadcom stock a buy?

At 28.3 times forward earnings, Broadcom isn't exactly a bargain-bin stock. Investors are still paying a premium for its growth prospects, and any slowdown in AI infrastructure spending could put additional pressure on shares.

title: These Were the Best-Performing Asset Classes in October. Will They Continue to Outperform?
detail:
These Were the Best-Performing Asset Classes in October. Will They Continue to Outperform?
Matthew Benjamin, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 10:50 AM MST 4 min read
^GSPC
GOOG
DELL
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It was an October to forget for the U.S. stock market. The S&P 500 index fell almost 1% during the month, but the carnage was particularly bad last week, when tech stocks tanked amid disappointing third-quarter earnings. Stocks such as Alphabet, Dell Technologies, and Intel saw double-digit losses during the week.

That said, which asset classes outperformed in October? More importantly, can they continue to do so heading into the last two months of 2026?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Surprisingly, real estate investment trusts (REITs) had a great month. They were up 4.8% in October, as measured by the Vanguard Real Estate Index Fund ETF (NYSEMKT: VNQ). That exchange-traded fund holds various types of REITs, including data centers, healthcare, industrial, and retail REITs, among others.

Commodities also had a good October. They rose 4.1% during the month, as measured by the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (NYSEMKT: GSG). The ETF tracks the S&P Dow Jones GSCI index, which is heavily concentrated in energy commodities. GSG doesn't have physical ownership of commodities, however. It gains exposure to them via futures contracts.

Crude oil prices drove commodity indexes higher during the month

If you look at the price of the leader of commodities, crude oil, it's no wonder that ETF did so well in October. Brent crude, the international benchmark, remained above $100 a barrel for the entire month due to ongoing tensions in the Persian Gulf.

Image source: Getty Images.

The question for investors now is: Can REITs and commodities continue their run?

At first glance, the strong performance by REITs was a bit surprising. While the Federal Reserve didn't hike its target rate at its October monetary policy meeting, interest rates are clearly headed higher in the coming months, with futures markets expecting two to three more quarter-point hikes by the end of 2027. Typically, that would be bad news for REITs, as real estate values tend to decline when interest rates rise.

But the correlation between REIT values and interest rates has weakened this year due to strong fundamentals among REITs -- solid cash flows, earnings, and balance sheets -- likely driven by a healthy U.S. economy. I see that continuing in the coming months, so I think REITs can continue to perform well, absent an unexpected shock to the U.S. economy.
